title: ENISA NIS360 - 2024
method: composite maturity/criticality index for 22 NIS2 Annex I (sub)sectors built from an industry survey (93% large firms; same fieldwork as NIS Investments 2024), a survey of national authorities, ENISA incident data (CIRAS) and Eurostat indicators
outcomes: sector cybersecurity maturity and criticality; 'risk zone' sectors
headline: Electricity, telecoms and banking score highest on maturity and criticality, while ICT service management, space, public administrations, maritime, health and gas fall in a 'risk zone' where maturity lags criticality.
summary_plain: ENISA's first sector-by-sector scorecard for the industries covered by NIS2. Long-regulated sectors like power, telecoms and banks are the best prepared; newly covered or weakly supervised sectors such as public administration, health and space are lagging.
quality: Baseline monitoring around the NIS2 transposition deadline; composite index with judgement-based weights, no counterfactual; industry data overlap with NIS Investments 2024
interested_party: ENISA is the EU agency charged with supporting NIS2 implementation

title: ENISA NIS360 (third edition; press release 'NIS360: The bigger picture on maturity and criticality of NIS critical sectors')
venue: ENISA report and press release, 28 May 2026
method: repeated composite maturity/criticality assessment of NIS2 Annex I sectors (entity surveys, national authority input, EU-level data), compared with the previous edition
outcomes: change in sector cybersecurity maturity; risk-zone membership
headline: Maturity improved across EU critical sectors since the previous edition: trust services, aviation and financial market infrastructures moved into the high-maturity band and gas, road, maritime and health improved within the moderate band, though health, railway, maritime, ICT service management, space, public administrations and water remain in the risk zone.
summary_plain: ENISA's latest scorecard finds critical sectors are getting better at cybersecurity as NIS2 takes hold, with several moving up a band. ENISA links part of the improvement to the new legislation, but progress is uneven and many sectors are still behind.
quality: Before/after comparison of a composite index with no control group; ENISA attributes improvement partly to NIS2 but cannot separate it from threat trends; only press release read
interested_party: ENISA is the EU agency charged with supporting NIS2 implementation

title: Companies Suffered Damage from Cyberattacks and Are Sceptical About NIS-2 (ZEW Information Economy Report Q4 2025)
method: representative business survey of about 1,100 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing (Dec 2025-Jan 2026), about 200 of which expect to be covered by NIS-2
outcomes: self-reported NIS-2 compliance; perceived burden; cyberattack damage
headline: About 57% of firms that consider themselves affected by NIS-2 say they already comply with most rules and 17% do not (fully) comply; around half expect it to strengthen cybersecurity, but about 60% call the administrative burden too high and reporting too extensive.
summary_plain: A large German survey run just after Germany's NIS-2 law came into force. Most affected firms say they mostly comply and half think it will help security, but most also say the paperwork and reporting are too heavy.
quality: Representative survey but only ~200 affected firms; self-reported, one country, right after transposition; press release only

title: NIS Investments 2022
method: survey of 1,080 operators of essential services and digital service providers in all 27 Member States, year-on-year comparison, sector deep dives (energy, health), plus Gartner market data
outcomes: IT and information security budgets; influence of the (first) NIS Directive on investment
headline: Third edition surveying 1,080 OES/DSPs: absolute IT and information-security budgets and the share of IT budgets spent on security were significantly lower than the previous year, partly due to sample composition and COVID-19.
summary_plain: ENISA's yearly survey of companies covered by the original NIS rules, tracking how much they spend on cybersecurity and how the law shapes that spending. It is part of the evidence base behind NIS2.
quality: Predecessor (NIS1) evidence that directly concerns NIS2's scope; self-reported, non-panel sample so year-on-year changes partly reflect composition
interested_party: ENISA is the EU cybersecurity agency

title: NIS Investments Report 2023
method: survey of 1,080 operators of essential services and digital service providers across the EU27 (fourth edition)
outcomes: cybersecurity budgets and how the NIS Directive influenced investment
headline: Fourth edition presenting data from 1,080 OES/DSPs in all 27 Member States on how they invest their cybersecurity budgets and how the NIS Directive influenced this investment.
summary_plain: The 2023 round of ENISA's survey of companies covered by the NIS rules, intended to show policymakers whether the EU cybersecurity framework is working, just before NIS2 had to be applied.
quality: Predecessor (NIS1) evidence and NIS2 baseline; self-reported survey, no counterfactual; landing page only
interested_party: ENISA is the EU cybersecurity agency

authors: Gardner, H., Enzerink, S., Page, M., Brincat, A. (Capgemini); Tenge, E., Velcsov, T., Macchioni, M.S. (Spark Legal and Policy Consulting); Lechardoy, L., Spolverato, G. (Open Evidence)
title: Study supporting the evaluation of the Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation, Open Data Directive and Data Governance Act - Final Report
venue: European Commission, DG CONNECT (Publications Office, published 12 January 2026)
method: ex-post evaluation: register analysis of notified data intermediation providers and data altruism organisations, surveys of national competent authorities, interviews with 9 providers, stakeholder surveys and focus groups, legal analysis
outcomes: uptake of data intermediation and data altruism; national implementation; burdens
headline: The DGA is at a 'nascent stage': by October/November 2025 only 27 data intermediation providers had registered in seven Member States (vs 100-150 expected; none in about three quarters of Member States) and only three recognised data altruism organisations existed.
summary_plain: The Commission's contracted evaluation finds that very few businesses or non-profits have signed up to the new trusted data-sharing schemes the act created. Delayed national implementation and unclear benefits of registering hold uptake back.
quality: Official ex-post evaluation; descriptive counts and stakeholder evidence, no counterfactual; small provider sample
interested_party: Commissioned and steered by the Commission (evaluating its own act)

authors: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A.
title: Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Belgium, France and Italy
method: difference-in-differences with propensity-score matching on firm accounts (3 years after signature), fixed-effects panel models, probit and Cox survival models
outcomes: SME growth in assets, sales, employment, fixed assets; labour productivity; survival
headline: Three years after the guaranteed loan, beneficiaries grew 8.0 pp more in assets, 5.4 pp in sales and 7.8 pp in employment than matched firms (all p<0.01), with labour productivity about 2% lower.
summary_plain: Small firms in Belgium, France and Italy that got bank loans backed by the EU's COSME guarantee grew faster in jobs, sales and investment than similar firms without one. The scheme is the direct predecessor of the InvestEU SME guarantee.
quality: Strong matched DiD on predecessor instrument (COSME LGF, now run under InvestEU's SME window); selection on unobservables possible
interested_party: Published by the EIF, which manages the guarantees

authors: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A.
title: Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Greece, Poland, Spain and Romania
method: difference-in-differences with propensity-score matching on firm accounts, fixed-effects panel models, probit and Cox survival models
outcomes: SME growth in assets, sales, employment, fixed assets; productivity; bankruptcy
headline: Beneficiaries outgrew matched firms by 13.3 pp in assets, 10.8 pp in sales and 9.2 pp in employment after three years, with no productivity change, and were 2.8 pp less likely to go bankrupt by end-2023.
summary_plain: In Greece, Poland, Spain and Romania, small firms with EU-guaranteed loans grew faster and were less likely to fail than comparable firms. This is evidence on the guarantee scheme that InvestEU continues.
quality: Strong matched DiD on predecessor instrument (COSME LGF); unobserved selection possible
interested_party: Published by the EIF, which manages the guarantees

authors: EIB Operations Evaluation Division (Bernabè, S., Benko, B. et al.; with Ramboll, GDCC, Panteia)
title: Evaluation of the European Fund for Strategic Investments
venue: EIB Operations Evaluation, Thematic Evaluation Report, June 2018
method: mixed-methods evaluation: portfolio data, original survey of Infrastructure and Innovation Window final beneficiaries, Commission survey of SME Window beneficiaries, case studies
outcomes: investment mobilised; additionality (would projects have happened without support)
headline: Surveys found 76% of SME-window and 67% of infrastructure-window operations would have stopped, shrunk or been delayed without EFSI-backed financing (81% for equity-type vs 63% for debt), and 98% of surveyed debt operations received inputs the market could not provide.
summary_plain: The EIB's own evaluators found that most projects backed by the Juncker Plan guarantee, InvestEU's predecessor, said they would have been smaller, later or cancelled without it.
quality: Predecessor (EFSI) evidence; self-reported counterfactual from beneficiary surveys, likely upward-biased; in-house evaluation

title: Contribution of the EDPB to the European Commission's evaluation of the Data Protection Law Enforcement Directive (LED) under Article 62 LED
method: synthesis of national data protection authorities' questionnaire replies on LED application (Jan 2022-Aug 2025)
outcomes: DPA supervision and advice under the LED, resources, scope issues
headline: DPAs have increasingly advised police and other competent authorities on data breaches and issued guidance, but national implementation needs strengthening, the role of DPOs should be reinforced, and DPAs and the EDPB lack financial and human resources.
summary_plain: Europe's data protection regulators report on how the police data protection law worked in 2022-2025. They have been more active, but say national laws still fall short and they lack the staff and money to supervise properly.
quality: Regulator self-reporting synthesised qualitatively; full PDF blocked (403), only press release read
interested_party: DPAs are the supervisory authorities under the LED and seek more resources

authors: EDRi (authors: Fitzjean Ó Cobhthaigh, A., Le Querrec, B., Korenke, C., Chelioudakis, E., Nikiforov, L., Križnar, P., Golla, S.)
title: Shadow evaluation report of the Law Enforcement Directive (2016/680) implementation
method: structured comparative country studies (Bulgaria, France, Germany, Greece, Slovenia) of transposition and practice on four themes, based on legal texts, DPA reports and case documentation
outcomes: data subject rights restrictions; sensitive-data safeguards; legal bases; use of new technologies
headline: Eight years after entry into application, implementation is highly fragmented and largely insufficient: all five Member States studied impose overly broad restrictions on data subject rights and none has a sufficiently detailed legal basis for big-data processing.
summary_plain: A digital-rights NGO checked how five countries apply the EU police data protection law and found gaps everywhere, especially in people's ability to see their data and in rules for big-data policing.
quality: Structured qualitative assessment, five countries, largely legal; no quantitative outcome data

authors: European Banking Authority & European Central Bank
title: 2025 Report on Payment Fraud
method: descriptive statistics on semi-annual PSP fraud reporting (PSD2 Art. 96(6) and ECB payment statistics), EEA, 2022-2024
outcomes: value and rate of payment fraud by instrument; SCA effectiveness
headline: EEA payment fraud rose from EUR 3.4bn (2022) and EUR 3.5bn (2023) to EUR 4.2bn (2024), stable at about 0.002% of transaction value; credit-transfer losses EUR 2.2bn (+16%) and card losses EUR 1.33bn (+29%).
summary_plain: Official figures on how much payment fraud happens in Europe. Totals are rising, especially scams where people are tricked into sending money, even though fraud remains a tiny share of all payments.
quality: Authoritative outcome monitoring for the Directive's target, but not attributable to the Directive (effects mainly linked to PSD2 SCA); press release read

title: Report on card fraud in 2020 and 2021
method: descriptive statistics from 20 card payment scheme operators, SEPA-issued cards
outcomes: card fraud value and rate; card-not-present and cross-border fraud
headline: Card fraud fell to 0.028% of card payment value in 2021 (EUR 1.53bn of EUR 5.40trn, vs EUR 1.87bn in 2019), with card-not-present fraud down 12% from 2020; cross-border transactions were 11% of value but 63% of fraud.
summary_plain: Card fraud in Europe hit a record low in 2021, around when the Directive had to be transposed, mostly thanks to stronger online payment checks.
quality: Outcome trend spanning the May 2021 transposition deadline; decline attributed by ECB to PSD2 SCA, not the Directive; press release read

authors: MedDMO (Mediterranean Digital Media Observatory; researchers incl. Sirivianos, M. and Andreou, A., Cyprus University of Technology)
title: Anonymous third-party paid political advertising in the Cyprus 2026 parliamentary elections
method: systematic monitoring of paid political content in Meta, Google and TikTok ad libraries/APIs (machine-learning search on 753 candidate and party names) from the TTPA application date
outcomes: political ads sold despite platform bans; anonymous sponsors; enforcement
headline: Five anonymous advertising operations ran more than 450 political ads in the final weeks of the campaign, and platform enforcement was largely reactive, after ads had reached large audiences.
summary_plain: After the EU's political-ad rules took effect and Meta and Google said they would stop selling political ads, researchers in Cyprus still found hundreds of election ads, some from anonymous sponsors spreading fake polls.
quality: Systematic measurement but single small election; detailed figures (e.g. 2,457 Meta ads, 887 TikTok ads) only via secondary report (Tech Policy Press); landing page read

title: What Data Reveals About Meta and Google's Political Ad Ban in the EU
method: descriptive analysis of TTPA self-disclosures on the Dutch politiekereclame.nl portal (65 campaigns) plus Meta Ad Library spending data
outcomes: quality of TTPA transparency disclosures; loss of ad-library data
headline: Of 65 Dutch election campaigns tracked under TTPA self-reporting, only 43 (66%) reported which media channels they used; the three largest without channel data represented over EUR 3.2m in spending.
summary_plain: A researcher looked at the first disclosures political advertisers made under the new EU rules in the Dutch election and found them patchy and unstandardised, while Meta and Google's exit removed the main public ad archives.
period_geography: Oct 2025; Netherlands (plus EU Meta spending since 2022)
quality: Small descriptive sample inside an opinion piece by an academic; early, one election

authors: Aplin, T., Radauer, A., Bader, M.A., Searle, N.
title: The Role of EU Trade Secrets Law in the Data Economy: An Empirical Analysis
venue: IIC - International Review of Intellectual Property and Competition Law
method: online survey of 84 organisations (Sept 2021-Mar 2022), 51 expert interviews, 13 case studies, from a study for the European Commission
outcomes: use of the Trade Secrets Directive to protect shared data; perceived gaps
headline: Drawing on a survey of 84 organisations, 51 interviews and 13 case studies, the authors conclude that only very modest reform of the Trade Secrets Directive is warranted to support data sharing, favouring soft law and practical steps.
summary_plain: Researchers asked companies and experts how the EU trade secrets law works when businesses share data. They found it broadly fit for purpose and recommend guidance rather than big legal changes.
quality: Small convenience sample, qualitative-heavy; no outcome measurement or counterfactual

authors: European Commission and national CPC authorities
title: Sweeps (coordinated screening actions under the CPC Regulation), 2020-2025 results
venue: European Commission, consumer protection enforcement web page
method: coordinated compliance audits ('sweeps') of websites by CPC authorities: e.g. 223 review sites (2021), 399 web shops for dark patterns (2022), 16,000 products/176 sites on Black Friday (2022), 576 influencers (2023), 356 second-hand traders (2024), 314 traders on price practices (2025)
outcomes: share of traders flagged as non-compliant with EU consumer law; cases earmarked for follow-up
headline: Sweeps repeatedly find high non-compliance: 55% of review websites (2021), 37% of web shops using dark patterns (2022), 97% of influencers posting commercial content but only 20% disclosing it (2023), and only 40% of traders fully complying with price-reduction rules on Black Friday 2025.
summary_plain: Under the cooperation regulation, consumer authorities across Europe check hundreds of websites at once for breaches. The checks keep finding that a large share of online traders break the rules, and flag them for follow-up.
quality: Output and compliance monitoring of the CPC network, not an impact estimate; screening results before enforcement; Commission reporting on its own network
interested_party: Commission coordinates the sweeps (reporting on its own network)

searched: Data Act survey/readiness, compliance evidence after Sept 2025, cloud switching/egress fee price studies, German business surveys (Bitkom, IW, ZEW, DIHK). Only the Bitkom 605-firm survey (already listed; its 'Data Economy 2025' PDF is the same survey) and a theoretical TSE model on egress fees; no ex-post empirical study.
new PLD survey/insurance/preparedness evidence; only law-firm commentary (Directive applies from Dec 2026).
Platform Work Directive employment effects, post-adoption evidence; only legal analyses, ELA legal study on misclassification and pre-transposition Fairwork ratings (not about the act).
Not searched beyond the existing list: the shared web-search budget ran out before this act was reached. Worth a follow-up (e.g. OpenSSF/Eclipse/Linux Foundation readiness surveys).
Not searched: the web-search budget ran out. IMERA has not been activated, so ex-post evidence is very unlikely.
